# Expressions

Edva programs are composed from expressions. Calls, bindings, choices, cycles,
and blocks all have expression forms. The generated
[operator table](../../../GRAMMAR.md#16-operators--precedence) is the single
precedence reference; this page describes how the principal forms fit together.

## Calls and application

Use `f(a, b)` for a direct call. `$` appends an argument to a call-shaped
function expression, while `$>` feeds a value into the first argument position.
Both are multi-argument operators, so pipelines can remain flat.

```dva
sum: Int, Int => Int
sum = left, right => left + right

first = sum(2) $ 3
second = 2 $> sum(3)
```

`$` is right-associative and `$>` is left-associative. Their right-hand side
absorbs a following choice, so parenthesize when a tighter interpretation is
needed.

## Choices, cycles, and assignments

A choice has adjacent guarded branches and an optional trailing bare fallback:

```dva
value = 2
label = value [1] "one" [2] "two" | "other"
```

One-branch choices are statements, not exhaustive values. A choice used as an
assigned or returned value must have meaningful compatible branch values; do
not add a dummy `| 0` fallback.

`@` iterates an iterable or range. `-->` breaks and `--^` continues the
current cycle; `>--` supplies an escape-expression branch. See the
[choices guide](../../guide/choices-and-cycles.qmd) for examples.

`=` creates or writes a binding according to its mutability. `+=` appends to a
Builder in place. A Builder length assignment has the special form `?builder =
n`. Every assignment evaluates to Unit. Expressions immediately after `=` and
choice conditions are written without surrounding parentheses. A function
returns its final expression's value, so a final assignment makes the function
return Unit; write `()` only as that type in a declaration, never as a value.

## Type-directed forms

`!` is flag negation (flags only; emits `E3008` on other types); `+` (unary prefix) freezes a Builder
into an immutable String in place; `&` (unary prefix) extracts a buffer address (`RawPtr`);
`?` measures the byte or element count of its operand; `++` copies strings, records, and
growable arrays. `!!` unwraps a positive ram payload or aborts on its negative slot.
Explicit scalar conversion uses call syntax such as `Int(rune)`. `<>(ram)` observes a ram's
polarity and returns a flag; it cannot convert one ram shape into another.
